questions.q: What does `plot_histogram(counts)` draw a bar for?
options: Every possible bitstring for the number of qubits, regardless of count
Only the bitstring keys actually present in the counts dictionary with a nonzero count
Only the single most frequent outcome
The gates applied in the circuit
questions.explain: plot_histogram draws one bar per key that appears in the counts dictionary. A bitstring with zero count and no entry in the dictionary produces no bar at all, not a zero-height one.

questions.q: For the Bell-state circuit (qc.h(0); qc.cx(0,1)) with the seeded draw {'00': 503, '11': 521, '01': 0, '10': 0} at shots=1024, what would plot_histogram(counts) actually show?
options: Four bars of roughly equal height
Two bars, for 00 and 11, both near the chart's mid-height, with no bars at all for 01 or 10
One tall bar for 11 and nothing else
Four bars with 01 and 10 shown at zero height
questions.explain: Only 00 and 11 have nonzero counts (503 and 521 out of 1024, both near 50%), so only those two bars are drawn. 01 and 10 are absent from the dictionary with zero count, so they simply don't appear.

questions.q: What does the x-axis of a plot_histogram chart represent?
options: Time elapsed during the run
The measured bitstring outcome, such as '00' or '11'
The qubit index
The shot number
questions.explain: Each position on the x-axis is a distinct measured outcome (bitstring); the y-axis gives its count or probability.

questions.q: How do you compare an ideal simulation's counts against a noisy hardware run's counts in one chart?
options: Call plot_histogram twice and visually overlay the two images yourself
Pass a list of counts dictionaries to plot_histogram, e.g. plot_histogram([counts_ideal, counts_hardware], legend=['ideal','hardware'])
Manually subtract one dictionary from the other first
plot_histogram cannot compare two runs
questions.explain: plot_histogram accepts a list of counts dictionaries and draws paired, legend-labeled bars per outcome, making differences between runs directly visible.

questions.q: For the Bell state, the theoretical probabilities are P(00)=0.5, P(11)=0.5, P(01)=P(10)=0. Why might two separate seeded 1024-shot runs show slightly different bar heights for 00 and 11 (e.g. 503/521 vs. 498/526) while 01 and 10 stay at exactly zero both times?
options: The circuit itself changes between runs

00/11 reflect real shot-to-shot statistical variation around the true 50/50 split, while 01/10 have zero probability under the circuit's entanglement structure, so no amount of resampling produces them on an ideal simulator
The simulator is broken
plot_histogram randomizes bar heights for visual appeal
questions.explain: 00 and 11 are the only outcomes with nonzero probability, so their exact split wobbles run to run due to ordinary sampling noise. 01 and 10 have true probability exactly zero on an ideal simulator, so they never appear regardless of how many times you resample.
